newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Seoul denies blocking imports with frugality drive.
newsitem.headline: Seoul denies blocking imports with frugality drive.

text.p: South Korean Finance Minister Kang Kyong-shik on Thursday rejected U.S. charges the government was sponsoring a "frugality" campaign targetting luxury imports from whiskey to cars.
"It is not true the government is leading such campaigns aimed at discouraging excessive consumption and imports," Kang told a news conference.
He criticised civic and religious groups whose campaigns against lavish consumption to combat a widening trade deficit have been taken up by the national media.
"Such campaigns will bring more losses than gains," he said, adding the government was concentrating its efforts on fighting waste and cutting down budget spending.
"I think it is not appropriate to target any specific luxury items or specific classes of people in these campaigns," Kang said.
His comments are among the clearest yet that the Korean government publicly is trying to distance itself from an anti-consumption campaign that it has promoted in the past.
Last month, the European Union and the United States attacked South Korea over its austerity campaign, suggesting the government was breaking global trading rules in a bid to reduce imports.

At a meeting of the World Trade Organisation's (WTO) Council for Trade in Goods, U.S. and EU officials called on Seoul to take a clear public stand on the issue which they said was having a serious impact on exports to one of their largest Asian markets.
Products targetted most severely in the frugality drive include cars, spirits, golf clubs, furs and cosmetics.
U.S. vehicle importers have complained of intimidation by traffic police and tax authorities of foreign car owners.
South Korean President Kim Young-sam, alarmed by a ballooning current account deficit, last year urged the nation to join a belt-tightening campaign and cut down spending on "luxury" items.
The word "luxury" in South Korea is often taken to mean "imported".
Foreign businesses argue that a drive against imports of consumer goods is misplaced, noting such imports account for only about 10 percent of total foreign purchases.

South Korea's current account deficit hit a record high $23.72 billion in 1996, up from $10.06 billion in 1995, mainly due to plunging global prices for exports and rising costs of imported raw materials.
Citizens' groups in South Korea have slammed EU and U.S. pressure as foreign meddling.
"We will boycott products from countries that put trade pressure on us," said Park Chan-sung, a leader of the Citizens' Movement Centre for Anti Over-Consumption.
"Our campaign has nothing to do with the government," he said. "It is aimed at saving the troubled economy by reducing unnecessary consumption."

EU and U.S. officials argue that government complicity is illustrated in a mounting incidence of "administrative harassment" by customs and other authorities against imports and owners of imported goods.
They say arbitrary use of standards, customs delays, or other measures to deter imports conflicts with WTO principles and obligations.
